subChunks.title: List & ArrayList — ordered, indexed collections
subChunks.hookHtml: A wizard's spellbook contains many spells — in a specific order, with a known position for each. Java's List interface and its star implementation, ArrayList, are your spellbook.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
List and ArrayList

List is an interface; ArrayList is the most commonly used implementation. It stores elements in insertion order and allows duplicates.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

List<String> spells = new ArrayList<>();
spells.add("Fireball");
spells.add("Ice Lance");
spells.add("Heal");
spells.add("Fireball"); // duplicates allowed

System.out.println(spells.size());    // 4
System.out.println(spells.get(0));    // Fireball
System.out.println(spells.contains("Heal")); // true

spells.remove("Ice Lance");  // remove by value
spells.remove(0);            // remove by index — removes "Fireball"
System.out.println(spells);  // [Heal, Fireball]

Iteration

// for-each (preferred — clean and safe)
for (String spell : spells) {
    System.out.println(spell);
}

// indexed for-loop (use when you need the index)
for (int i = 0; i < spells.size(); i++) {
    System.out.println(i + ": " + spells.get(i));
}

List.of() — immutable lists

List<String> fixed = List.of("A", "B", "C"); // cannot add/remove

Sorting

import java.util.Collections;
Collections.sort(spells); // alphabetically

import java.util.Comparator;
spells.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)); // by length

ArrayList vs LinkedList

Use ArrayList (default) — O(1) random access. Use LinkedList only when you need O(1) insertions at both ends (a queue/deque), as it has O(n) random access.

storyBeats.text: Eldrin drops an ancient spellbook on your desk — pages dog-eared, spells numbered and indexed.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Arrays have a fixed size — you declare them with a length and that is it. But what if you don't know in advance how many spells you'll collect? Enter ArrayList — a dynamic, ordered list that grows as needed.

storyBeats.speaker: Building a spellbook
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice: we declare the variable as List<String> (the interface), not ArrayList<String>. This is program to the interface — a key principle. It means you can swap ArrayList for any other List implementation later without changing anything else.

storyBeats.speaker: Iteration and sorting
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: When you need a list that nobody can change, use List.of(). It throws an UnsupportedOperationException on any mutation attempt. Excellent for configuration data or constant lookup tables.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a spell-inventory system:

  1. Create an ArrayList<String> and add these spells: "Meteor", "Blizzard", "Fireball", "Heal", "Teleport".
  2. Print the size.
  3. Print the spell at index 2.
  4. Remove "Blizzard" by value.
  5. Sort the list alphabetically.
  6. Print each spell using a for-each loop.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a List is in Java's Collections Framework. When would you use ArrayList vs LinkedList? What does 'program to the interface' mean, and why is it a good practice?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From a blank file, create a grade tracker:

  • Create a List<Integer> called grades with these values: 88, 72, 95, 61, 84, 90, 77.
  • Print the total count.
  • Calculate and print the average (cast to double for precision).
  • Sort descending (hint: Collections.sort(grades, Collections.reverseOrder())).
  • Print the highest grade (index 0 after sort).
  • Remove any grade below 70 using a removeIf lambda: grades.removeIf(g -> g < 70).
  • Print the count of passing grades remaining.

questions.questionHtml: Which method adds an element to the end of an ArrayList?
questions.explanationHtml: list.add(element) appends to the end. list.add(index, element) inserts at a specific position, shifting elements right.
remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes the first element equal to 1 (at index 1). remove(1) with an int would remove by index. After removal: [3, 4, 1, 5].

questions.questionHtml: A List returned by List.of() can have new elements added to it.
questions.explanationHtml: List.of() returns an immutable list. Calling add(), remove(), or set() throws UnsupportedOperationException.

options: When you need fast random access by index
When you need frequent insertions and deletions at both ends (queue/deque use case)
When you need to sort the list frequently
questions.correctAnswer: When you need frequent insertions and deletions at both ends (queue/deque use case)
questions.explanationHtml: LinkedList offers O(1) insertions/deletions at the head and tail (it implements Deque), making it ideal for queue and stack operations. ArrayList has O(1) random access (get(i)) but O(n) insertions in the middle. In practice, ArrayList wins for almost all use cases due to better cache locality.

subChunks.title: Set & Map — unique elements and key-value pairs
subChunks.hookHtml: Sometimes you need uniqueness — a set of visited rooms in a dungeon. Sometimes you need lookup — a character's stats by name. Java's HashSet and HashMap are the go-to tools for both.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Set — no duplicates

HashSet is the most common implementation. Order is not guaranteed.

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

Set<String> visited = new HashSet<>();
visited.add("Library");
visited.add("Dungeon");
visited.add("Library"); // ignored — already present

System.out.println(visited.size());       // 2
System.out.println(visited.contains("Dungeon")); // true

Use LinkedHashSet to maintain insertion order; use TreeSet for sorted order.

Map — key-value pairs

HashMap stores entries as key → value pairs. Keys are unique; values can repeat.

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

Map<String, Integer> stats = new HashMap<>();
stats.put("health", 100);
stats.put("mana", 80);
stats.put("strength", 45);

System.out.println(stats.get("mana"));      // 80
System.out.println(stats.containsKey("agility")); // false

// Safe get with default
int agility = stats.getOrDefault("agility", 0); // 0

// Iterating entries
for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> entry : stats.entrySet()) {
    System.out.println(entry.getKey() + ": " + entry.getValue());
}

Map operations

stats.put("health", 150);     // overwrites existing key
stats.remove("strength");     // removes entry
stats.putIfAbsent("agility", 30); // only adds if key not present

// Merge: add 10 to existing mana, create with 10 if absent
stats.merge("mana", 10, Integer::sum); // mana: 90

Choosing the right collection

NeedUse
Ordered sequence with duplicatesList / ArrayList
Unique elements, fast lookupSet / HashSet
Key-value lookupMap / HashMap
Sorted unique elementsTreeSet
Sorted key-valueTreeMap

storyBeats.text: Eldrin hands you two enchanted ledgers. The first has a wax seal that refuses to record the same entry twice. The second is a lookup table — name on the left, stat on the right.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The first ledger is a HashSet. You add an element; if it's already there, it is silently ignored. Perfect for tracking which dungeon rooms you have explored — no duplicates, O(1) lookup.

storyBeats.speaker: HashSet — visited rooms
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The second ledger is a HashMap. Every entry has a unique key and a value. Look up a wizard's health by name in O(1) time — regardless of how many wizards are registered.

storyBeats.speaker: HashMap — character stats
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: To iterate a Map's entries, use entrySet(). It gives you both the key and value together. Iterating only keys: keySet(). Only values: values().

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a simple word-frequency counter:

  1. Create a List<String> of words: "the", "wizard", "cast", "the", "spell", "the", "wizard".
  2. Use a HashMap<String, Integer> to count how many times each word appears. Use map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) or getOrDefault approach.
  3. Print each word and its count.
  4. Use a HashSet to print the number of unique words.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between List, Set, and Map in Java. Give a concrete real-world scenario where you'd choose each one, and explain why.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From a blank file, build a phonebook:

  • Create a HashMap<String, String> mapping names to phone numbers. Add at least 5 entries.
  • Look up two names: one that exists, one that doesn't (use getOrDefault to return "Not found").
  • Update one existing entry's phone number.
  • Remove one entry.
  • Print all remaining entries using entrySet() in the format "[name]: [number]".
  • Create a TreeMap from the HashMap and print its keys — observe they are sorted alphabetically.

questions.explanationHtml: A Set guarantees uniqueness — adding a duplicate element has no effect. HashMap ensures unique keys, but that is different from Set semantics.
Putting a value with an existing key overwrites the previous value. So "a" maps to 99. The map still has 2 entries ("a" and "b").

questions.questionHtml: What does map.getOrDefault("key", 0) return if "key" is not in the map?
questions.explanationHtml: getOrDefault(key, defaultValue) returns the mapped value if present, or the default value otherwise. It never throws an exception and never returns null (unless your default is null).

questions.questionHtml: You need to count the occurrences of each word in a document and retrieve the count for any word in O(1) time. Which data structure is most appropriate?
questions.explanationHtml: A Map<String, Integer> maps each word (key) to its count (value). Lookup by key is O(1) in a HashMap. A List would require O(n) scanning to find a word. A Set only tracks presence, not count.
